name: Victor Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Hollis Farm for Ruth Hollis, who's 71 and still lives in the farmhouse. It's 400 hectares of wheat, oilseed and grass, plus about 90 beef cows with calves. I run two staff, Dev and old Frank. Most days I'm out on the tractor or in the cattle yard by seven, and the paperwork happens at the kitchen table after dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that Ruth trusts me with the whole place. She'll say, Victor, you decide, and she means it. What wears me out is the forms. Every grant, every spray record, every cattle movement has a form. I've started using an AI chat tool now and then to draft the grant letters, and it's saved me a few evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's all it is. At the union branch I'd tell people to stop panicking and start asking for better pay, since the bosses can't claim the robots are coming. Online I'd probably post a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much changes for me. My job is muddy boots and judgement calls, and that stays. I'd be a bit disappointed, actually, because some of the forms really could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chat tool for grant letters, maybe once a week. I'd keep putting money aside and keep the flat I rent out in town. I'd ask Ruth about a pay rise for Dev, who's earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a forecast for rain that never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chat tool saved you a few evenings. Would you keep using it here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for the boring stuff. I checked the first letter it wrote line by line, and it had the grant rules a year out of date. So I use it, but I read every word. That's how I am with most new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be arguing about at the union in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay and housing for farmworkers, same as always. Half the young ones on farms round here live in caravans. That's a bigger problem than AI in this picture.

S0.say: It's a useful tool and that's all it is. At the union I'd tell people to stop panicking and start asking for better pay, since the bosses can't claim the robots are coming.
S0.think: Not much changes for me, because my job is muddy boots and judgement calls. I'd even be a bit disappointed, because some of the forms really could go.
S0.do: Keeps using an AI chat tool about once a week for grant letters, checking every line. Keeps saving and keeps his rented-out flat, and asks the owner for a pay rise for his worker Dev.
S0.quote: I checked the first letter it wrote line by line, and it had the grant rules a year out of date.
S0.fieldNote: Victor treats AI as a careful user would: useful, but checked. His politics come out straight away in his concern for farmworkers' pay and housing. He seems almost disappointed that the paperwork wouldn't shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where unions earn their money. Change is coming, so let's make sure workers share in the gains and get trained. I'd say it at the branch and probably write something for the union newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine and my two staff might not be. A good farm manager is still needed in this picture. But a robot that can spot-spray weeds or push feed in the cattle yard takes hours off Dev and Frank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the neighbours buy for a season before I touch anything. The Okafors next door always go first, so I'd learn from their mistakes. I'd do a short course on farm software in the winter, probably the one at the agricultural college, which costs a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about other people. For myself, more curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the farm would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weeding and feeding. The weed-spotting sprayers already exist, the Okafors have one on trial. If it works on their wheat, Ruth will ask me about it by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dev and Frank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank is 63 and he'd love to retire anyway, he talks about his allotment every lunch. Dev is the one I'd worry about. He's 22 and he's only ever done this. I'd push to keep him and train him on the new kit instead of letting him go.

S1.say: This is where unions earn their money. Change is coming, so workers should share in the gains and get trained, and I'd write that in the union newsletter.
S1.think: I think I'm fine as a farm manager, but my two staff might not be. Robots that spot-spray weeds or push feed would take hours off them.
S1.do: Watches the neighbouring farm's trials for a season before buying anything. Takes a winter course in farm software at the agricultural college for a few hundred, and pushes to keep his young worker Dev and train him on new machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy for others, curious for himself.
S1.quote: The Okafors next door always go first, so I'd learn from their mistakes.
S1.fieldNote: His steady approach shows clearly: let the neighbours test it, then follow. His worry points outward to Dev, a 22-year-old with no other experience. There is a quiet confidence about his own place that he doesn't say loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now, not after. If machines can do all the work, the gains have to be shared, through taxes, public ownership, whatever it takes. I'd be marching, probably, which I've done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Ruth sells. She's 71, she has no family in farming, and a company would offer her a fortune for a farm that runs itself. Then I'm a manager with nothing to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, maybe half my pay, and stop the plan to buy a second flat. I'd join the union campaign for a tax on robots that pays into a fund for workers. I'd use the AI tools a lot more, every day, because if it's coming in two years I can't wait for the Okafors to test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sam would notice before me, she always does. I'd get short-tempered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth, the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her straight out what she plans to do with the farm. We've never talked about it. I'd ask whether she'd consider leaving part of it in a trust for the workers, or selling to a co-op, before a big company gets there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long for someone who likes to see things proven first. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. I'd have to break my own habit and jump before it's proven. The rental flat and savings give me a couple of years of room, so I'm not desperate. But I'd hate jumping blind.

S2.say: Governments need to move now, not after. If machines can do all the work, the gains have to be shared through taxes or public ownership, and I'd be marching for it.
S2.think: I think Ruth sells, because she's 71 with no family in farming and a company would pay a fortune for a farm that runs itself. Then I'm a manager with nothing to manage.
S2.do: Saves about half his pay, shelves the plan to buy a second flat and joins a union campaign for a robot tax that funds workers. Starts using AI tools every day and asks the owner directly about selling to a co-op or a workers' trust.
S2.feel: Anxious and short-tempered, though savings and the rental flat give him some room.
S2.quote: I'd have to break my own habit and jump before it's proven.
S2.fieldNote: The threat to him runs through the owner's choice to sell, not through his own skill. Two years forces a steady man to act like an early adopter, and he dislikes it. His instinct is a collective fix: a workers' trust or a co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a five-year emergency and should be treated like one. Rules on who owns the robots, retraining paid for publicly, help for small farms to buy in together. I'd say it calmly but often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to land on my feet. Probably not as a farm manager. Maybe running the machines, or managing a group of farms that share robots. I'd be fine. Dev's the one who worries me again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd learn what the robot dealers are selling and try a small one on Hollis Farm. I'd sit down with Ruth and the Okafors about sharing machines. I'd keep saving a third of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. Five years is long enough that I could get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with the fast one you'd hate jumping blind. Does five years fix that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'd get two or three years to watch it working on other farms. That's my natural speed. In the fast one I'd be guessing, here I'd be choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam over dinner, the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're okay. Her school job might even outlast mine, kids still need a person in the room. Then I'd probably go quiet and do the sums in my head.

S3.say: This is a five-year emergency and should be treated like one, with rules on who owns the robots, public retraining and help for small farms to buy in together.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to land on my feet, maybe running the machines or managing a group of farms that share robots. Dev is the one I'd worry about again.
S3.do: Learns what robot dealers are selling and trials a small robot on the farm in year one. Talks with the owner and neighbours about sharing machines, and keeps saving a third of his pay.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, because five years fits his habit of watching before acting.
S3.quote: In the fast one I'd be guessing, here I'd be choosing.
S3.fieldNote: For Victor, the difference between two and five years is the difference between guessing and choosing. Five years matches his natural pace. He reassures his partner out loud and does the sums silently, a small gap between say and think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Train people now, write the rules now, and don't let three companies own all the machines. I'd keep saying that at the union until people were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years catches me right in the middle. I'd be 37, maybe with kids, and the thing I'm best at would stop being needed. It's not a crisis, but it's the wrong time of life for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next few years getting a qualification in farm robotics or land management, probably part-time over two winters. I'd keep the flat and maybe sell it later to put money into a share of a farm. I'd want to be an owner of something by then, even a small piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough off that I can plan, close enough that I can't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 37 you'd be in the middle of your career. Is ten years better or worse for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, honestly. Two years would hit me before I'd done anything. Ten gives me time to become someone who owns the robots instead of being replaced by them. But I'd have to actually do it, and I know I like to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be farming in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be on the land, yes. Maybe not driving the tractor. But I'd still want to walk the fields in June and decide when the wheat's ready.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if we use it: train people now, write the rules now, and don't let three companies own all the machines.
S4.think: Ten years catches me right in the middle, at 37 and maybe with kids, just as the thing I'm best at stops being needed. It's not a crisis, but it's the wrong time of life.
S4.do: Studies part-time over two winters for a qualification in farm robotics or land management. Keeps his rental flat with a view to selling it later to buy a share in a farm.
S4.feel: Uneasy: far enough away to plan, close enough not to ignore.
S4.quote: Ten gives me time to become someone who owns the robots instead of being replaced by them.
S4.fieldNote: He wants ownership, even a small share, which sits interestingly beside his left-leaning politics: he'd prefer co-ops but he'd still buy in. He's honest that his habit of waiting could waste the decade. The image of walking the fields in June shows what he's actually attached to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Not because of me, I'd manage, but because Ruth would sell before anyone had a plan and people like Dev would be out with nothing. What would help is a public fund, paid for by taxing the robots, that helps workers buy into farms together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the land. Everyone talks about the robots, but the robot just works for whoever owns the field. If that's three big companies, it doesn't matter how clever the machine is, the village dies.

headlineQuote: The robot just works for whoever owns the field.
portrait: Victor Chen is a 27-year-old farm manager running 400 hectares of crops and beef cattle for an elderly owner who trusts him completely. He's left-leaning, careful with new tools, and uses AI only now and then for grant letters, checking every line. Through the five pictures his main worry is not his own skill but whether the owner sells and what happens to his young worker Dev. More warning time suits his habit of watching before he acts, and with ten years he wants to become a part-owner rather than be replaced.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the owner would sell before anyone had a plan and workers like Dev would be left with nothing.
whatWouldHelp: A public fund, paid for by taxing robots, that helps workers buy into farms together.
